Kristian Andersen, PhD: The Andersen lab studies how dangerous pathogens emerge, spread, and evolve in human populations, focusing on diseases like SARS-CoV-2, Zika, Ebola, West Nile, and Lassa virus. They combine next-generation genomic sequencing, on-the-ground field work, laboratory experiments, and computational biology to trace outbreaks in real time, often through large international collaborations. A well-known example of this work is their analysis tracing the early spread of COVID-19 to a market in Wuhan, and their research showing mpox had quietly circulated in Nigeria for years before its international outbreak. The goal is to understand the biology of host-pathogen interactions well enough to improve disease surveillance and outbreak response. This lab would suit students interested in genomics, epidemiology, virology, or computational approaches to public health, especially those drawn to fast-moving, collaborative science with real-world stakes.
Ahmed Badran, PhD: The Badran lab uses synthetic biology and protein engineering to tackle environmental and biomedical problems. A major thread of their work is inspired by how plants capture carbon dioxide: they are engineering the photosynthetic enzyme RuBisCO to improve how efficiently plants pull CO2 from the atmosphere, aiming to help offset the effects of fossil fuel use on climate and agriculture. They also develop new molecular biology tools, including methods that expand the genetic code by using four-letter RNA sequences instead of the natural three to build synthetic protein components. Their broader interest is engineering the core molecular machines that make life work, both to discover new medicines and to design climate-relevant biotechnology. Students interested in synthetic biology, protein engineering, or the intersection of chemistry and environmental science would find this lab relevant.
William Balch, PhD: The Balch lab studies how genetic variation across human populations affects the way proteins fold, and how misfolding contributes to disease and aging. They combine experimental techniques from cell biology, biochemistry, and structural biology with computational and machine-learning tools (including Gaussian Process models) to analyze protein structure and function at the level of individual amino acids. A specific focus is the cellular quality-control machinery (chaperone systems like Hsp70 and Hsp90) that manages whether proteins fold correctly. Their work has shown, for example, that some genetic diseases can potentially be corrected not by fixing the mutated gene itself but by controlling how the resulting protein folds. The lab aims to build a general framework for understanding and eventually treating diseases caused by protein misfolding. Good fit for students interested in computational biology, protein science, or genetic disease mechanisms.
Phil Baran, PhD: The Baran lab works in organic chemistry, developing new and more efficient ways to synthesize complex molecules, including natural products and pharmaceuticals. Their central idea is 'ideal synthesis': building complicated molecules in as few steps as possible, avoiding wasteful protective chemistry, and using radical (rather than only classical polar) chemical reactions. They have dramatically shortened the number of steps needed to make certain natural products and have invented widely used chemistry tools, such as reagents for late-stage modification of molecules and a platform for building therapeutic oligonucleotides. The lab also helped popularize modern organic electrochemistry, including co-developing a widely adopted lab device for electrochemical reactions. Their methods are applied across drug discovery, agrochemicals, and materials science. This lab suits students interested in hands-on synthetic organic chemistry with direct applications to medicine and industry.
Donna Blackmond, PhD: The Blackmond lab develops and applies methods for figuring out how chemical reactions actually work at the molecular level. Their signature technique, Reaction Progress Kinetic Analysis (RPKA), uses precise real-time measurements of a reaction as it happens, combined with mathematical analysis, to work out reaction mechanisms from scratch rather than just confirming an existing hypothesis. This approach is used to study important reaction types in pharmaceutical chemistry, including catalytic and asymmetric reactions, and has become a standard tool in industrial drug development. The lab also investigates the origin of 'biological homochirality' — why life uses only one mirror-image form of molecules like amino acids — through kinetic studies and experiments on how chiral molecules behave in solution. Students interested in physical/organic chemistry, reaction mechanisms, or the chemical origins of life would find this lab a good match.
Michael Boddy, PhD: The Boddy lab studies how cells detect and repair damage to their DNA, and how failures in this process contribute to cancer and premature aging. They use a mix of cell biology, proteomics, genetics, and structural biology to understand the molecular machinery involved. A major discovery from the lab was a new family of proteins called STUbLs, which revealed how two cellular tagging systems (SUMO and ubiquitin) work together to manage DNA damage responses, with direct relevance to how certain leukemia therapies work. More recent work has shown that some DNA repair proteins can mimic other cellular signals to hijack these pathways, a finding that connects to both cancer biology and how cells defend against viruses. This lab would appeal to students interested in molecular biology, genome stability, or cancer mechanisms.
Dale L. Boger, PhD: The Boger lab is a synthetic organic chemistry lab focused on designing and building complex molecules with medical applications, especially in the face of rising antibiotic resistance. A major project involves redesigning vancomycin, a critical antibiotic, to create new 'maxamycin' compounds with added mechanisms of action that are more durable against resistant bacteria. The lab has also developed total synthesis routes for natural products like vinblastine, contributed new chemical methods (such as reactions using tetrazine compounds), and worked on treatments for chronic pain and an experimental cancer vaccine. Their broader approach connects fundamental synthetic chemistry with real therapeutic problems. Students interested in medicinal chemistry, drug design, or the chemistry behind fighting antibiotic-resistant infections would find this lab a strong fit.
Michael Bollong, PhD: The Bollong lab works on regenerative medicine, aiming to develop drugs that activate the body's own capacity to repair damaged tissue rather than just manage disease symptoms. They combine traditional drug discovery methods with modern biological techniques to identify and target the molecular pathways that control tissue regeneration. Their research targets a range of conditions including heart disease, inflammatory disease, and fibrosis (scarring) of organs like the lungs. Through Scripps' drug discovery arm, Calibr-Skaggs, the lab's science has advanced to human clinical trials, including an inhaled drug designed to regenerate lung stem cells in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This lab would interest students drawn to translational medicine, drug discovery, or the biology of tissue repair and regeneration.
Bryan Briney, PhD: The Briney lab studies antibodies, the immune proteins that recognize and fight viruses, with the goal of guiding vaccine design. Their work includes comparing antibody repertoires (the full diversity of antibodies a person or animal can produce) using high-throughput sequencing, and identifying rare, protective antibodies against dangerous viruses like HIV, Lassa, and coronaviruses. By analyzing the structures of antibody-virus complexes across different viral lineages, the lab has helped pinpoint new targets for vaccines and antibody-based therapies. Their research is part of larger collaborative efforts aimed at stockpiling protective antibodies and designing vaccines against future pandemic threats. This lab would suit students interested in immunology, vaccine science, or the genetics of the immune system.
Dennis Burton, PhD: The Burton lab studies broadly neutralizing antibodies — rare immune antibodies capable of fighting off many different strains of highly variable viruses like HIV and coronaviruses. The lab pioneered methods for isolating and characterizing these antibodies, mapping exactly where on a virus's surface they attack, and using that information to guide vaccine design. Their findings have moved from basic antibody discovery through animal testing and into human clinical evaluation, carried out through large NIH- and Gates Foundation-funded research consortia. This work underlies major efforts toward an effective HIV vaccine and informs strategies against influenza and coronaviruses more broadly. Students interested in immunology, virology, or vaccine design, especially the antibody side of the immune response, would find this lab directly relevant.
Sergio Catz, PhD: The Catz lab studies how cells move materials internally through a process called vesicular transport, focusing on a family of proteins called Rab GTPases that organize this trafficking. Using super-resolution microscopy and functional lab assays, they study how vesicular transport controls processes like autophagy, immune cell secretion, and the clearance of pathogens by immune cells such as neutrophils. Their research connects these basic cellular mechanisms to human diseases, including coronary artery disease, lysosomal storage disorders, and autoimmune conditions like lupus. The lab has also built high-throughput screens to discover small-molecule drugs that can adjust vesicular transport, some of which are being tested in preclinical disease models. This lab suits students interested in cell biology, immunology, or drug discovery targeting basic cellular machinery.
Sumit Chanda, PhD: The Chanda lab studies how viruses interact with human cells and how the innate immune system responds, with a particular focus on RNA viruses that carry pandemic risk (such as coronaviruses, influenza, and dengue). Using systems-level and cutting-edge screening approaches, they identify how the body detects and fights these viruses, then use those findings to drive drug discovery through Calibr, Scripps' translational research arm, developing new antivirals, vaccine adjuvants, and immunotherapies. The lab's work is funded by major organizations including the Gates Foundation and NIH, and involves partnerships with pharmaceutical companies. They are also part of the team behind Metascape, a widely used bioinformatics tool for analyzing gene lists. This lab would suit students interested in virology, immunology, or translational antiviral drug discovery.
Michael G. Constantinides, PhD: The Constantinides lab studies how the immune system's 'first responder' cells, called innate lymphocytes, protect barrier tissues like the skin and gut lining, and how they interact with the trillions of microbes (the microbiota) that live there. Their research looks at how microbes shape the development and function of these immune cells, and in turn how the immune cells help regulate the microbial communities, using this two-way relationship to understand immune health. The lab is working to develop targeted approaches to manipulate these interactions as a route toward new therapies for infectious disease, autoimmunity, and cancer. Beyond the science, the lab emphasizes mentorship and expanding access to science for students from underrepresented backgrounds. This lab would suit students interested in immunology, microbiome science, or barrier tissue biology.
Candice Contet, PhD: The Contet lab studies the brain mechanisms behind alcohol's behavioral effects, particularly what drives excessive drinking and the transition to alcohol dependence. One line of research examines specific potassium channels (GIRK and BK) that alcohol activates directly, testing their role in intoxication, tolerance, and chronic drinking using genetically engineered mice. Another line studies brain circuits involving the neuropeptide CRF and a brain region called the parasubthalamic nucleus, which influence motivated behaviors related to alcohol use. The lab also uses untargeted proteomics to search for new molecular contributors to excessive drinking. They combine mouse behavioral models with electrophysiology, mass spectrometry, and bioinformatics, often in collaboration with other labs, aiming ultimately to develop better treatments for alcohol use disorder. Students interested in neuroscience, addiction biology, or behavioral pharmacology would find this lab a strong match.
Benjamin Cravatt, PhD: The Cravatt lab develops chemistry-based technologies to understand what proteins actually do in the body and to find new drug targets. Their signature method, activity-based protein profiling (ABPP), measures whether an enzyme is functionally active in cells and tissues, rather than just how much of it is present, since activity — not abundance — is often what matters for disease. ABPP also serves as a broad platform for discovering small molecules that can bind and control specific proteins, expanding the range of proteins that can be targeted with drugs. Alongside this technology development, the lab studies specific enzymes relevant to the nervous system and cancer, such as FAAH and MAGL, which break down cannabinoid-like signaling molecules. This lab would suit students interested in chemical biology, drug discovery, or neuroscience-related enzymology.
